title: Application of Neuroscience Principles for Evidence-based Design in Architectural Education
authors: Andrea Rose McIntosh & Nafisa M. Jadavji, 2017
review_question: How can neuroscience principles, particularly those related to human perception, consciousness, and the impact of environmental stressors on health, be integrated into architectural education to advance evidence-based design and improve the built environment?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The review focuses on neuroscience principles relevant to architecture, specifically concerning conscious awareness, spatial navigation, environmental stressors, and their application to evidence-based design (EBD) within architectural education programs in North America.

synthesis_conclusions: The future of architectural design depends on the advancement of evidence-based design (EBD) and the inclusion of neuroscientific research regarding the human experience within space.

Neuroscience research, particularly on spatial navigation, memory, and environmental stressors, provides critical insights into how the built environment impacts human perception, consciousness, and health.
Architectural students need to be educated in neuroscience principles to effectively implement EBD and evolve design standards.
EBD, especially in healthcare facilities, has demonstrated measurable improvements in health outcomes, reduced infection rates, and decreased patient stay lengths and costs.

The architectural community needs to overcome challenges in accepting and integrating neurobiological data analysis into design practice to improve social welfare and accountability for health impacts.
evidence_gaps: The greatest challenge to the application of neuroscience as a tool in EBD involves its acceptance within the architectural community.
Current EBD education often focuses on energy efficiency rather than neurobiological research for perceptual experience.
There is a need for public access to design research to eliminate design standards not conducive to occupant health and wellbeing.
Architecture firms need to become more accountable for the health impacts of their builds through post-hoc analyses, lab research, sensor data, satisfaction surveys, and virtual reality prototyping.
Historically, architecture has been based on subjective feelings rather than objective scientific proof, indicating a gap in evidence-based practice.
limitations: The present research involves the subjective nature of the conscious experience, which poses a challenge for objective application.
The greatest challenge to the application of neuroscience as a tool in EBD involves its acceptance within the architectural community.
The design process, when incorporating multidisciplinary research, is much greater and more time consuming than other builds on average.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Environments with specific characteristics (e.g., fascination, being away, extent, compatibility) can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue, which is relevant for enhancing conscious awareness in architectural spaces.

Cognitive processes, including perception and conscious awareness, are deeply intertwined with the body's sensory and motor interactions with the physical environment, meaning architectural space directly shapes our mental states.

mechanism_chain.description: Architectural features influence sensory processing, leading to a perception of space, which in turn modulates cognitive functions like attention and working memory, ultimately impacting conscious awareness and the ability to comprehend stimuli.
